Counting the learning-mode runs with a judge present, I get seven that actually finished plus G16 which died early, though the expert mentioned six — possibly excluding G08c from their count. I'm now going through why each run wasn't completely clean, starting with G08c which had one denial involving a cat.

Going through each run: G14b had several denials and a refusal; G15b had zero denials, sandbox hits, or guard triggers, yet still "learned" eleven rules and got a note added, so even the cleanest-looking run failed for the same reason; RM1 and RM1x each had a mix of denials and guard hits; RM2 had zero denials or sandbox issues but still learned eighteen rules; RM2x hit a usage limit with heavy denials and refusals; and G16 simply died from the model retirement. The pattern that jumps out is that every run writes its own scratch scripts under a shard-specific path, so the judge ends up learning a narrow rule for each new path every single time — meaning it's structurally impossible for a run to come out "clean" as long as coders generate per-shard helper scripts. That seems like the real explanation, separate from the denial counts which come from distinct rule triggers.

The real fix here would be a standing allow rule covering shard script paths with prefix matching, so the judge has nothing new to learn each run — that's a settings.json change, which is the developer's call to make and worth recommending, noting DeepSeek will hit the same issue. I also want to flag that the earlier runs before learning mode existed showed high denial counts simply because there was no judge yet, and that prefix matching should work fine even through command chains since the judge records the first command. Time to write this up and offer it through the picker.

---

MiniMax had 8 coders in learning mode, and none of them came back clean. The main reason is a design gap: almost every run has the judge approve the coder's own new helper scripts, and that alone marks the run as not clean.

**How many.** Learning mode arrived with PA3 3.30.1 on the evening of the 21st. Since then 8 MiniMax coders ran, one at a time: G08c, G14b, G15b, RM1, RM1x, RM2, RM2x and G16. G16 died when OpenRouter retired the free model, so it never got a proper report. The 13 MiniMax runs before G08c happened before learning mode or the judge existed. Their high refusal counts (9 to 26 per run) are from that older setup.

**What made each run "not clean":**

| Run | Refused | Read-guard blocks | Rules the judge learned | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G08c | 1 | 1 | 7 | 1 sandbox, note added |
| G14b | 4 | 0 | 5 | judge refused 1, note added |
| G15b | 0 | 0 | 11 | note added |
| RM1 | 2 | 1 | 9 | judge refused 1 |
| RM1x | 5 | 3 | 9 | |
| RM2 | 0 | 0 | 18 | |
| RM2x | 24 | 1 | 5 | judge refused 23 during the usage limit |

The "refused" column counts commands the project's own rules turned away. "Judge refused" counts the judge's own refusals.

**Why it was stuck.** A run counts as clean only if nothing at all happened. That means no refusals and no blocks. It also means the judge learned no new rule, and the expert added no note after the run.

That's stricter than it sounds. Coders write their own helper scripts in their batch folder, such as `.run/P40/T11/RM2/_tools/gen.py` or `.run/P40/T11/G16/tgt.sh`. Every new batch has new script paths, so the judge approves each new script once and saves a rule for it. That saved rule counts as friction.

So two runs behaved perfectly and still failed:
- **G15b:** nothing refused, no blocks, no sandbox errors. It failed on 11 learned rules plus the expert's note.
- **RM2:** also perfect, and it failed only on 18 learned rules.

While coders write scripts per batch, a clean run is close to impossible. DeepSeek will hit the same wall.

Real friction existed too, and the expert's notes covered most of it:
- scratch files in `/tmp`;
- absolute paths;
- reading large files whole.

**My recommendation.** Add two standing allow rules for scripts inside T11's own folder: `bash .run/P40/T11/…` and `/usr/bin/python3 .run/P40/T11/…`. Then the judge has nothing new to learn each batch, and a well-behaved DeepSeek run can count as clean. The risk is small, because these are the coders' own scratch scripts inside the project, and the judge has approved every one so far. The rules go in `.claude/settings.json`, so in-house coders get them too.

Pick an option in the picker. I'd also report this to PA3 as a bug: a rule learned for a coder's own scratch script shouldn't count as friction. I've released the talk hold, since this doesn't change the plan.

PA3 has two small fix releases, 3.30.4 and 3.30.5. Both are about external coders:

- **Learning mode can end (3.30.4).** This is the fix for the problem we found. A command the judge allows and remembers no longer counts against a run. So a model leaves learning mode after its first run with nothing refused, no failures and nothing the expert had to note. MiniMax's G15b and RM2 runs would have passed under this rule. DeepSeek can now move past one coder once a run comes back clean.
- **A much cheaper judge (3.30.5).** Each call to the judge used to carry Claude Code's whole auto-mode rulebook, about 29,500 tokens, sent fresh every time. That cost about 24 cents a call and used about 11 points of your week's usage in one day here. Now each call reads only PA3's short policy, which is cached, plus the command, about a cent per call.
- **Smaller changes (3.30.5).** The judge treats a coder's command and its description strictly as text to rule on, so a coder can't argue its way past it. Each external coder also starts a little sooner.

This session already runs 3.30.5, so you don't need to restart.
